name: James son of Zebedee
title: One of the Twelve
tagline: A fisherman’s son from Galilee; the one apostle Scripture says was put to death.
story: Son of Zebedee, brother of John and a fisherman; one of three Jesus took aside, and the one apostle Scripture says was put to death.

entries.title: Fishing near Capernaum
entries.text: Scripture does not name their town. They were fishing on the sea of Galilee near Capernaum when called, and went with Jesus to the house of Simon and Andrew there (Mark 1:19–21, 29).

entries.title: In his father’s boat
entries.text: Fishermen in their father’s boat on the sea of Galilee (Matt 4:21; Mark 1:19–20), “partners with Simon” (Luke 5:10).

entries.title: Son of Zebedee
entries.text: Son of Zebedee, who was in the boat with his sons mending nets when Jesus called them, and who had “hired servants” (Matt 4:21; Mark 1:20).

entries.title: His mother’s request
entries.text: Their mother is “the mother of Zebedee’s children”, who asked Jesus for the places at his right and left (Matt 20:20–21) and watched the crucifixion from afar (Matt 27:55–56).

entries.title: Salome? An inference
entries.text: Mark names “Salome” where Matthew has “the mother of Zebedee’s children” among the women at the cross (Mark 15:40; Matt 27:56). Taking her to be Salome is an inference from comparing the two lists; our people data makes it.

entries.title: Cousins of Jesus? A view
entries.text: Some writers go further and make Salome the sister of Jesus’ mother (John 19:25), which would make James and John cousins of Jesus. Camerlynck (1910) reports this and judges that “the relationship of St. James to Jesus remains doubtful”.

entries.text: He is named second among the Eleven in the upper room (Acts 1:13).

entries.title: Killed with the sword
entries.text: “Herod the king” kills “James the brother of John with the sword” (Acts 12:1–2).

entries.title: Clement of Alexandria, Hypotyposes book 7, quoted by Eusebius (2.9.2–3)
entries.text: The man who led James to the judgment seat was moved by his testimony, confessed himself a Christian, asked James’s forgiveness and received “Peace be with thee”; “thus they were both beheaded at the same time.” Clement tells it “as he received it from those who had lived before him”.

entries.title: Spanish tradition, as assessed by A. Camerlynck
entries.text: James preached in Spain, returned to Judea to be killed, and his body was carried to north-west Spain and later to Compostela. Camerlynck notes that the tradition was current by about 700, but “the first certain mention” is in the 9th century.

claim.text: His brother, called with him and named with him as Boanerges (Mark 1:19; 3:17).
A fishing partner (Luke 5:10), and with John one of the three at Jairus’s house, the transfiguration and Gethsemane (Mark 5:37; 9:2; 14:33).
His father, left in the boat “with the hired servants” (Mark 1:20).
She asked that her two sons might sit at Jesus’ right and left (Matt 20:20–21).

scripture.text: When James and John asked for the places of honour, Jesus told them, “Ye shall indeed drink of the cup that I drink of” (Mark 10:39).

“Now about that time Herod the king stretched forth his hands to vex certain of the church. And he killed James the brother of John with the sword” (Acts 12:1–2). Of the Twelve, he is the only one Scripture says was put to death.
Acts tells his death just before Peter’s arrest, which it sets in “the days of unleavened bread”, and before Herod’s own death at Caesarea (Acts 12:3–4, 19–23).
Camerlynck (1910) dates the death to the Passover of AD 44, the year in which Herod Agrippa I died.

items.q: Did James preach in Spain before he died?
items.full: Did James preach in Spain before he died?

views.label: Yes, the Spanish tradition
views.holders: Writers from the 9th century on (Notker, Walafrid Strabo); defended by the Bollandists

argument.text: Camerlynck reports the tradition and that the Bollandists defended it in the Acta Sanctorum.

views.label: Doubtful
views.holders: The objections as summarised by A. Camerlynck (1910), who says “numerous scholars reject it”

argument.text: James died in AD 44 in Jerusalem (Acts 12:2), and early writers say the apostles had not yet left Jerusalem. Paul, planning to visit Spain, says he would not “build upon another man’s foundation” (Rom 15:20, 24). No early writer or council mentions it.

argument.text: Four men called James appear in our people data. This is the son of Zebedee and brother of John (Matt 4:21), not James son of Alphaeus (Matt 10:3) or James the Lord’s brother (Gal 1:19).

items.from: The identifications this page relies on

argument.text: The name “James the Greater” is a later way of telling him from James son of Alphaeus; Scripture does not use it.

items.from: The identifications this page relies on

argument.text: Jesus “surnamed them Boanerges, which is, The sons of thunder” (Mark 3:17). Scripture does not explain the name.

items.q: John’s Gospel never names James; it mentions only “the sons of Zebedee” (John 21:2).
Scripture does not say why Herod chose James, or where he was buried.
Scripture does not give his age or say whether he was older or younger than John.
